title: Post-CTS congestion in SRAM channels on 28nm block
design_context: 28nm node, 1.0M placeable instances, 82 SRAM macros, 4 clock domains, commercial P&R
observation: First detailed-route attempt fails with 18% overflow concentrated in channels between SRAM macros M42-M45 and M58-M61; layers M6-M8 showing >15% overflow in these channels while other regions remain <3%
hypothesis: Post-CTS optimization increased logic density around SRAM channels without adjusting macro placement, creating routing bottlenecks in the macro-to-macro channels

candidates_considered.action: Re-run global placement with congestion-aware cost weight increased from 0.4 to 0.9
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Adds 1.5 days to schedule with no guarantee of fixing channel-specific hotspots given fixed macro positions

candidates_considered.action: Swap SRAM macros M42 and M65 to open channel between M42-M45 cluster
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Requires re-running timing for both macro domains (estimated 1.0 day CPU) and risks breaking existing timing closure in both domains

candidates_considered.action: Manually add routing guides around congested channels
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Requires manual creation of 50+ guides, error-prone and not scalable; estimated 0.8 days of engineer time

chosen_intervention: Local halo expansion of 5% around congested SRAM clusters M42-M45 and M58-M61, plus pin access optimization on 25 cells in hotspot, followed by incremental detailed routing
expert_assessment: Correct call for schedule constraints. Lesson: post-CTS optimizations can create local congestion that global placement won't fix. Does not transfer to designs with <5% global overflow where global re-placement is viable.
weakest_point: The exact timing degradation from halo expansion is tool-dependent and may vary by 10-30ps

title: Spatial clustering of 12k failing paths reveals physical congestion, not constraint issue
design_context: 28nm node, 900K placeable instances, 75 macros, 3 clock domains, commercial P&R
observation: 12000 timing paths failing by 20-50ps each, slack histogram shows tight clustering (std dev 12ps), 85% of failing paths originate or terminate in top-right quadrant of the block, no common clock domain
hypothesis: Physical congestion in top-right quadrant causing excessive wirelength and capacitance on nets in that region, systematically degrading timing for all paths routing through it

candidates_considered.action: Relax setup constraint by 10% across the block
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Would mask real timing issues in other quadrants, risking silicon failure in non-congested regions

candidates_considered.action: Upsize all drivers on failing paths
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Increases area by 0.8% and power by 3.0%, plus creates new congestion in an already-tight top-right quadrant

candidates_considered.action: Re-synthesize logic in top-right quadrant only
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Requires 2 days of runtime and could introduce new timing violations while not addressing the physical routing cause

chosen_intervention: Re-run placement with congestion-aware cost function focused on top-right quadrant (weight 1.2), followed by incremental timing optimization limited to that region
expert_assessment: Excellent diagnosis from spatial clustering. The geographic concentration was the telltale sign of a physical/placement problem. Lesson: always plot failing path locations on the floorplan before assuming logic or constraint issues. Would not have worked if the slack distribution was bimodal.
weakest_point: The exact improvement from congestion-aware placement is flow-dependent and tool-specific

title: Async boundary budget derived from measured clock skew and uncertainty
design_context: 28nm node, Block A: 800K instances, Block B: 600K instances, async boundary, commercial P&R
observation: 180 paths crossing A-to-B boundary failing by 100-250ps, all setup violations with no hold violations, failures correlate with launch clock domain CLK_A
hypothesis: Missing timing budget at async boundary; current SDC assumes ideal clock alignment and zero uncertainty between CLK_A (Block A) and CLK_B (Block B)

candidates_considered.action: Set fixed budget of 200ps for all A-to-B boundary paths
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Overly conservative for 60% of paths, would cause unnecessary optimization effort and area increase estimated at 1.5%

candidates_considered.action: Mark all A-to-B boundary paths as false paths
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Would break functional timing for real synchronous handshake paths and cause silicon failure on boundary registers

candidates_considered.action: Use clock period difference (5.0ns) as budget
candidates_considered.rejected_because: Ignores clock uncertainty and jitter, which account for 150ps of the observed failures; would still leave 100ps of violations unaddressed

chosen_intervention: Derived budget = measured_clock_skew(100ps) + max_uncertainty(50ps) + 15% margin(22.5ps) = 172.5ps; applied as set_clock_uncertainty -setup 175ps on A-to-B boundary; set_clock_uncertainty -hold 80ps for hold checks
expert_assessment: Textbook derivation. Measuring actual skew with the clock tree analysis tool was the right first step. Lesson: always derive boundary budgets from real clock network metrics, not from period differences. Method fails if clock networks are not yet stable or if margin percentage is miscalculated.
weakest_point: The 15% margin is arbitrary and should be validated against historical data
